Elara’s workshop smelled of brass filings and old oil, a scent that had seeped into her very pores over forty years of service. She was a woman of precision, her hands steady as stone, her eyes sharp as needles. But today, her hands trembled. On the workbench lay the *Chronos Inversus*, a timepiece unlike any she had ever crafted. Its face was a mirror of polished obsidian, and its hands, made of silver wire, moved with a sinister, counter-clockwise grace.

Elara had built it not out of curiosity, but out of grief. Three months ago, her husband, Julian, had died in a sudden, senseless accident. The world had continued its relentless forward march, indifferent to her shattered heart. In her desperation, she had sought a way to undo the final moments, to pull the thread of fate back before the snap, before the fall. She believed that if she could reverse time, even for a second, she could save him.

The clock ticked. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* But the sound was wrong. It was a soft, sucking exhale rather than a sharp inhale. The dust motes in the air began to swirl, not falling, but
